segments.title: The bad day and the window
sections: The Day That Ends The Account

cues.text: The first trade wins. The next one comes a little faster, from a little further from your level.
Then one loses, and the next is taken to get it back.
By late morning what you saw at 9:30 was right, and the day is gone anyway.
An edge is a rule's advantage after costs. If you have one, it shows up in your record over months of trades. One bad day can take the account before that record exists.
So the five hard rules are not there to make you money. They are there so you are still trading when your record is big enough to judge. They predict nothing about price.
Here are the five. One: the trading window, the hours you may trade.
Two: the news windows, the minutes around big scheduled releases.
Three: four reasons to flatten by hand, which means to close a position yourself.
Four: the kill switch, your daily loss limit.
Five: the post-loss reset, a routine you run after every losing trade.
The first four are enforced by a clock, a calendar or a platform setting. A platform setting has one great quality. It cannot be talked into anything.
Now, rule one. The trading window is the hours in which you may place a trade: 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern.
Inside it sits the focus block, 9:30 to 11 a.m.
That is the first stretch of the cash session, the regular stock-market hours, when your levels, the price zones you marked before the session, meet the most traffic.
Nothing new is entered from 3:55 p.m. The last five minutes are for closing, not opening.
Before 9:30, you may trade only once the pre-market sheet, the one page you fill in before every session, is complete. No completed sheet, no trade.
The rule: no execution outside 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, and no new entries from 3:55 p.m.
Getting it wrong is one trade at 4:20 because the level was right there. In your journal, the record of every trade, it is tagged Broke Rule, and winners get the tag too.
It reveals a trade that came from the screen, not the plan. The fix: the window is the first line of your plan, with an alarm at 3:55.

segments.title: News windows and four exits
sections: Rule 3: Four Reasons To Flatten By Hand

cues.text: Some scheduled releases move index futures in a way no level survives. Rule two sorts them into two tiers.
Tier One is the releases you stand aside for. Inflation first: CPI, PPI and PCE.
Then the jobs report, NFP. The Fed's rate decision, FOMC. And Retail Sales.
Tier Two is the releases you manage through: home sales, the EIA energy report and consumer sentiment.
Plus the JOLTS job-openings report, and Fed speakers.
Now, the clock. Call the release time T. Around a Tier One number, price can jump through your stop, the order that closes a losing trade.
A position held through CPI is a coin toss with a stop attached. The stop is only a suggestion.
So be flat at T minus 5, with no open position and no resting orders, the ones waiting in the market. No new entries until T plus 2.
The rule: Tier One, flat at T minus 5, no entries until T plus 2. Tier Two, manage through.
Getting it wrong takes two forms. Holding through Tier One reveals a bet on the release. Exiting for Tier Two reveals a trader who wanted a reason to leave.
The fix: write each Tier One time on your plan with its T minus 5 and T plus 2. A position still open at T minus 5 is Broke Rule.
Now, rule three. A manual flatten is closing a position yourself, before its stop or its target, the price it aims for, has done it. Four reasons, and only four.
One: the stop was hit. If price traded through it and the order did not fill, you close by hand.
Two: a Tier One release is within five minutes.
Three: your thesis, the if-then behind the trade, broke on a candle close. That is the invalidation you wrote at entry.
Four: the session is over. It is 4 p.m. Eastern.
The rule: four reasons to flatten by hand. Every other manual exit is logged Too Early.
Getting it wrong is an exit that is none of the four: it stalled, or a red candle looked big.
It gets the Too Early tag, and its execution mark, the pass or fail you give every exit, is Fail.
The fix: write one of the four reasons beside every manual exit. Count the Too Early ones each week.

cues.text: This rule is counted in R, so the unit comes first. R is the fixed amount you risk on one trade, chosen before the trade.
Every outcome in the journal is in R, so trades of different sizes compare on one scale.
Now, the switch. The kill switch is your daily max loss: 2R, twice that amount. When the day's loss reaches it, trading stops until the next session.
It is fixed: never raised during the session, never adjusted after it fires. It ends the session and nothing more.
Now, where it lives. It only works if your hand cannot undo it at 10:40, so it belongs outside the window you trade from.
NinjaTrader 8, or NT8, has no daily loss limit. Its Risk window is for simulation accounts only.
On NinjaTrader Brokerage, set the Daily Loss Limit in the Dashboard's Risk Settings, and turn on Prevent Changes When Trading is Locked, so you cannot raise it that day.
On Tradovate, turn on the Daily Loss toggle, and Lock Risk Settings if Hit.
On Rithmic, the account provider sets the limit, not you. Write 2R in your plan anyway, with the words: written, not enforced.
A funded or evaluation account usually carries the firm's own limit. Treat it as a backstop, not your switch.
Two things the limit does not do.
One: it does not cap the loss exactly. It fires a market order, filled at the next available price, which can be past your number.
Two: it may not see an open loss. Some venues count realized loss only, meaning closed trades, so your resting stop bounds the open one.
A loss limit is a smoke alarm. It is loud, and it arrives after the smoke.
When it fires, the account goes liquidation-only: positions closed, resting orders cancelled, only orders that reduce a position accepted.
Then three steps. One: note the time and kill switch in the journal.
Two: close the platform.
Three: step away from the desk.
The rule: daily max loss is 2R, fixed, set at the account level with the lock on.
Getting it wrong is raising the limit at 10:40, or opening a second account. It reveals a trader trying to win the day back.
The fix is the lock, turned on before the session, so a calmer you decides.

cues.text: The first four rules are enforced by a clock, a calendar and a setting. This one is enforced by you, which is why it comes last.
The post-loss reset is a fixed routine, run after every losing trade and before any new entry. It is short and rehearsed, so it runs on a bad day without having to be remembered.
Now, the routine. Three parts. First, the cancel: every working entry order, an order still waiting to open a trade. One placed before the loss belongs to the trader you were before it.
Second, the physical step. Feet flat on the floor. One long exhale. Then three or four rounds of box breathing: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four.
Third, three questions, answered aloud.
One: what is the chart telling me?
Two: are any setups forming? A setup is a level and a read together: where you trade, and what price has to do there.
Three: what would need to happen for a setup to present itself?
Answer in sentences. Price is back inside the prior session's range and nothing is at a level: that is an answer.
It's going to come back is not an answer. It is a prayer with a ticker. If you cannot answer clearly, the next trade waits.
Now, the loop. This rule exists to stop the re-entry loop: entries taken one after another without a fresh setup.
It usually starts with a win, and each trade comes faster, from further from a level.
There is no cap on trade count in this course. The 2R switch is the cap, and the reset is the brake before it.
The journal shows your trade count per session, so you can see the loop for yourself.
The rule: after every loss, the full reset before any new entry.
Getting it wrong is an entry within a minute of a loss, or an old resting order that fills during the reset. It reveals a trade that came from the last trade, not from the chart.
The fix: before the next entry, write the answer to question three in one line in the journal. A blank line means no trade.
Rehearse it once on a quiet day, with no position on, so the first run is not the day you need it.

cues.text: This is a composite session with invented prices, built to show how the rules interact. It is a hypothetical illustration, not a trade record.

Hypothetical results have inherent limits: they are not actual trading and do not reflect real fills, slippage or the pressure of risk, and no representation is made that any account will achieve similar results.
The pre-market sheet is complete at 7:40. CPI is at 8:30, so T minus 5 is 8:25 and T plus 2 is 8:32.
The kill switch is 2R, at the account level, lock on.
Now, the session. At 7:58 a planned trade is open. At 8:25, five minutes before CPI, it is flattened by hand: reason two of the four.
At 8:32 entries return. Nothing is at a level, so nothing is taken.
At 9:56 a second planned trade reaches its stop. The trader runs the full reset and writes the third answer down.
At 10:41 a third planned trade reaches its stop. With fees, the day's loss is past 2R, and the limit fires.
At 10:42 the pull to re-enter is strong. The trader notes it, closes the platform and leaves the desk.
Now, what the rules did. Neither loss was a mistake. Both were planned trades, and the rules never asked them to win.
The one decision left to the trader came at 10:42, and the lock had already made it.
The market stayed open after 10:42. It does that. What price did next is not your money.
Now, your score. Five lines, each 2, 1 or 0. Two: a mechanism enforces it. One: you enforce it by hand. Zero: neither.
Line one, the kill switch: at the account level, with the lock on.
Line two, the window: on your plan, with an alarm at 3:55.
Line three, the news: every Tier One time written with its T minus 5 and T plus 2.
Line four, manual flatten: each of your last ten manual exits carries one of the four reasons, or Too Early.
Line five, the reset: rehearsed, and the third answer written after every loss.
The threshold: any zero is fixed before your next session. Under 7 out of 10, the rules are a wish, not a system.
Getting it wrong is scoring a 2 for good intentions. A 2 is a mechanism.

cues.text: Your assignment. Before you trade again, set your daily loss limit at the account level at 2R, with the lock on, or confirm that it already is.
If your venue lets you set no limit, write this line at the top of your next plan: Kill switch, 2R. At 2R, close the platform. That is the whole assignment.
Getting it wrong is setting the limit and leaving the lock off. A limit you can raise at 10:40 is not a rule. It is a nice thought.
The summary. Every one of these rules removes a decision from the worst moment to make it.
The window, the news times, the four reasons and the 2R limit are decided before the session. The reset is how you get back to the person who decided them.
Where it goes next. Every manual exit now gets an execution mark in the journal, pass or fail.
Module 18, Journaling and Review, teaches the mark and the weekly count of Too Early exits, and shows trade count per session, where a re-entry loop shows up as a cluster.
Module 3, The Instrument: Futures Mechanics, covers ticks and points, the steps price moves in, and what each is worth: the arithmetic that turns 2R into the figure you type into the setting.

questions.q: What are the hard rules for?
options: Keeping you trading until your record is big enough to judge
questions.why: They predict nothing about price; they decide how long a bad day can last and what it can cost.

questions.q: Which entry breaks the trading window rule?
questions.why: Nothing new is entered from 3:55 p.m.

questions.q: When must you be flat for a Tier One release?
questions.why: Flat at T minus 5, no new entries until T plus 2.

questions.q: A working trade is nearly at target and a Tier Two print is coming. What do you do?
questions.why: Tier Two: manage through, and never exit a working position because of it.

questions.q: Which manual exit is logged Too Early?
options: A stop hit that did not fill
questions.why: Anything outside the four reasons is Too Early, with an execution mark of Fail.

questions.q: The daily kill switch is set at...
options: Whatever you feel like each morning
questions.why: 2R, fixed, never raised during the session.

options: False: it holds simulation templates; live accounts use the broker's Dashboard
False: the limit lives on the chart
questions.why: NT8 has no daily loss limit of its own; the venue sets it.
